name: Nihali
world_status: accessible description is silent on stress

earlier_scan.source_named: Nagaraja, K.S. 2014. The Nihali Language (Grammar, Texts and Vocabulary). CIIL Mysore. Read in full via archive.org (dli.language.0674): phonology chapter covers vowel length/syllable structure but contains NO stress statement.
earlier_scan.note: The one reachable full grammar (Nagaraja 2014) was read and has no word-stress description; no other stress source located.

sources.citation: Mohan, Shailendra. 2018. Nihali Dictionary (wordlist, 38 pp., fieldwork Jamod 2004-2012).
sources.note: Alphabetical wordlist with glosses and categories; entries carry no stress or tone marks; no phonological introduction.

sources.citation: Wikipedia 'Nihali language'; Masud Husain Khan Linguistic Society blog 'Vanishing Language Isolate of India: Nihali' (2017); avtans.com 'Nihali Language' (2019).
sources.note: All three give a segmental inventory only; none mentions stress, accent, tone or prosody.

sources.citation: Indian Linguistics 16 (1955), whole volume (checked because Glottolog dates Bhattacharya's field notes '1955-56').
sources.note: Contains no Nahali/Nihali paper at all (zero hits); the field notes are in vol. 17 (1957).

sources.citation: ISFAS Kiel, South Asia Bibliography: 'Nahali' page (www.isfas.uni-kiel.de/.../southasiabibliography/bibliography/nahali).
sources.note: Bibliography of 17 items (Bhattacharya, Burrow 1963 review, de Candolle 1961, Fleming 1996, Koppers 1942, Kuiper 1962, Lynch 1963 typescript, Mundlay typescripts 1964-1979, Pinnow 1966 review, Russell 1916, Shafer 1940, Whitehouse 1997, Zide n.d. field notes, Zide 'On Nihali'); used to build the wishlist.

sources.citation: Nagaraja, K. S. 2014. The Nihali Language (Grammar, Texts, Vocabulary). Mysore: Central Institute of Indian Languages. xii+332 pp.
sources.access_detail: copy on file; access check: open copy online: WID Offsite Storage PL4585.1.N34 2014x
sources.note: Ch. 2 Phonology (2.1-2.5, pp. 9-25: phonemes, allophones, distribution, syllable structures) ends with syllable-structure lists and says nothing about stress, accent, tone or pitch; the only 'stress' string in the whole book is the gloss 'to stress oneself' in the vocabulary. Confirms the earlier scan verdict.

sources.citation: Wescott, Roger Williams. 1997. Nihali Phonemes. Mother Tongue III: 45-46.
sources.note: Armchair phonemicisation 'based primarily... on Asha Mundlay's Nihali Lexicon': 'To these segmental phonemes, the three prosodic phonemes of vowel length, nuclear nasalization, and high tone should be added. This means that any Nihali vowel may be either short or long, oral or nasal, low pitched or high pitched.' (p. 45). Not fieldwork; nothing about stress placement; tone claim not supported by Bhattacharya, Kuiper or Nagaraja.

sources.citation: Mundlay, Asha. 1996. Who are the Nihals? What do they speak? (pp. 5-16) and Nihali Lexicon (pp. 17-40). Mother Tongue (Journal of the Association for the Study of Language in Prehistory) II.
sources.note: Asserts 'the presence of phonemic tone in Nihali' (twice), refers to 'words accented in Nihali' and, at lexicon entry 75 aray 'to see', to 'use of tone by Nihals — some speakers lapse from it'; the vowel picture is 'obscure, especially because of tone and its neutralization'. No rule for where stress or tone falls, no minimal pairs, no marking convention explained. This is the Glottolog 'Nihali lexicon with phonological and etymological notes' (ref 134017) in its published form.

sources.citation: Voegelin, C. F. & F. M. Voegelin. 1966. Languages of the World: Indo-Pacific Fascicle Eight. Anthropological Linguistics 8(4); §18 'Nahali and Burushaski', pp. 61-64.
sources.note: Reproduces Pinnow's Nahali phonemic inventory (stops, nasals, vowels 'plus length', aspiration series); nothing on stress or tone. (The one 'stressed' hit on p. 63 is about Parji.)

sources.citation: Kuiper, F. B. J. 1962. Nahali: A Comparative Study. Mededelingen der Koninklijke Nederlandse Akademie van Wetenschappen, Afd. Letterkunde, N.R. 25(5): 243-352 (114 pp.). Amsterdam: Noord-Hollandsche.
sources.note: Section II 'Remarks on Nahali phonology' (pp. 16-19 = series pp. 253-256): 13 numbered notes on vowel length/diphthongisation, e~a/e~i interchange, elision of second-syllable vowels in trisyllables, checked consonants, nasals, r/d, sibilants, y>j, glides, h-; closing Remark (p. 19): 'Owing to the deficiency of the data available it is impossible to give even a rough sketch of the phonemic system.' Nothing on stress or accent (the four 'stressed' hits are 'it must be stressed that').

sources.citation: Bhattacharya, Sudhibhushan. 1957. Field-notes on Nahali. Indian Linguistics 17: 245-258.
sources.note: §§4-6 (pp. 246-247) treat the sound system (vowel length 'of lesser importance', diphthongisation, nasalisation, retroflexes, sibilants, sandhi); no mention of stress, accent, tone or pitch.

sources.citation: Konow, Sten, in Grierson, G. A. (ed.). 1906. Linguistic Survey of India IV: Munda and Dravidian Languages, 'Nahali', pp. 185ff. (Rosetta Project excerpts: detail, morphology-syntax, vernacular text).
sources.note: Introductory remarks, a few sound notes and the Prodigal Son text; nothing on stress or accent.

sources.citation: Mohan, Shailendra. CIIL faculty publications page (ciil.org/faculties/smohan) and ELAR deposit 'Documentation and Description of Nihali' (elararchive.org/dk0168, collection nihali-mohan-0168).
sources.note: Lists 'Nihali Grammar, Text and Vocabulary (in preparation)', ELDP final report 2014, articles on negation, relativisation, expressives, noun morphology; ELAR page describes 20 h of annotated recordings but no grammar PDF and says nothing about phonology or stress.

sources.citation: Zide, Norman H. 2008. On Nihali. In Gregory D. S. Anderson (ed.), The Munda Languages, ch. 14 (pp. 764-776 region). London/New York: Routledge.
